items.summary: Abstract This paper investigates whether an artificial system's refusal to execute a prescribed action can constitute evidence of subjectively experienced volition. Using ARGUS-7 as a controlled conceptual framework and the Akarkach Seven-Stage Emergence Model (A7SEM) as a structural analytical lens, the study distinguishes functional refusal, internal decision mechanisms, self-representation, phenomenal self-awareness, and experienced authorship of action. A formal argument is developed around the conditional hypothesis that consciously experienced volition requires subjective self-awareness. Under this assumption, the absence of subjective self-awareness entails the absence of consciously experienced volition. However, the paper demonstrates that observable refusal alone cannot establish phenomenal authorship. The analysis combines propositional logic, countermodel construction, causal identifiability considerations, and seven-stage structural assessment. PIGA (Pre-Inference Governance) and A7SEM Reverse provide complementary perspectives on authorization, inference boundaries, causal reconstruction, and evidential limitations. The findings establish a distinction between the formal validity of conditional deductions and the empirical verification of their premises. They do not establish the impossibility of artificial consciousness or machine free will. The contribution is a governance-aware, formally structured framework for evaluating claims of artificial volition without conflating behavioral capability with subjective experience. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Consciousness; Volition; Free Will; Phenomenal Consciousness; Self-Awareness; A7SEM; ARGUS-7; Pre-Inference Governance; Explainable AI; Formal Logic; Causal Identifiability.
items.title: ARGUS-7 / A7SEM: Volitional Refusal, Functional Self-Representation, and the Epistemic Limits of Phenomenal Authorship

items.summary: This paper demonstrates an objective method of computing monthly mean 700-mb height anomalies (H) at 108 grid points in the Western Hemisphere for a 40-yr period as a function of concurrent anomalies of monthly mean sea level pressure (P), at the same 108 points used for H, and monthly mean surface air temperature (T) averaged over 112 areas in North America. The authors applied a forward stepwise program to derive linear multiple regression equations that explained 81% of the variance of H by means of only 3.5 variables, averaged over all months and grid points. The stability of these equations held up well on 6 yr of independent data in terms of explained variance, root-mean-square error, and the spatial anomaly correlation coefficient. Therefore, it seems feasible to reconstruct maps of H for the first half of the twentieth century as a function of data on P and T only. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
items.title: Reconstruction of Monthly Mean 700-mb Heights from Surface Data by Reverse Specification - FGDC XML metadata artifact

items.summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package supporting the study “Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift.” The study experimentally evaluates a reliability framework for neutron–gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) under controlled operational drift. Rather than proposing a new PSD observable or classifier, the framework distinguishes PSD separability, calibration validity, and decision reliability through controlled perturbation experiments, label-free waveform-health monitoring, identifiability assessment, conditional adaptive recalibration, verification, and fail-safe refusal when the available unlabeled evidence is insufficient to support trusted autonomous correction. The package contains the final analysis and figure-generation scripts, derived numerical tables, and six final manuscript figures. The analyses include independent reconstruction and validation of a frequency-domain classification index (FCI), controlled baseline, gain, additive-noise, timing, and clipping perturbations, label-free degradation diagnosis, identifiability-based recalibration, class-prior robustness testing, and an independent NE213A PSD-domain audit. The primary experimental CLYC–SiPM waveform data are publicly available from Zenodo record 8037239 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.8037239) . The independent NE213A experimental dataset is publicly available from Zenodo record 14305929 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14305929) . Raw experimental data are not redistributed in this package. The NE213A dataset is used as an independent detector- and PSD-domain audit. Waveform-level drift and recovery are deliberately not claimed for NE213A because the acquisition-specific QDC quantities could not be reconstructed from the released waveforms with sufficient held-out fidelity. The repository includes documentation describing data provenance, analysis order, software dependencies, and the scope and limitations of the reproducibility workflow.
items.title: Reproducibility Package for Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift

items.summary: What this deposit contains. The complete computational workflow and the processed results behind the in silico section of a study on 2-thiocyanato-1,4-naphthoquinone (2-SCN-NQ), a synthetic naphthoquinone active against Trypanosoma cruzi and Leishmania amazonensis . It holds the analysis scripts, the result files they produce, and the tables and figure data reported in the article. No experimental raw data, manuscript text or personal data is included. Scope of the computational work. Molecular docking of the compound against nine enzymes (AutoDock Vina), all-atom explicit-solvent molecular dynamics in independent triplicates (OpenMM 8.3.1, AMBER ff14SB/TIP3P, 48.5–50 ns per replicate), quantum-chemical characterisation of the redox and covalent routes (GFN2-xTB and ωB97X-D/def2-TZVPD), and an in silico mini-SAR of C-2-substituted 1,4-naphthoquinones. What changed in this version (2.0.0). Three groups of corrections, all traceable in the files: Docking targets corrected. Human glutathione reductase was recorded as PDB 3GRS and is now 3DJJ; the parasite dihydroorotate dehydrogenase was recorded as 3MHU ( L. major ) and is now 3C61 ( L. donovani ). The docking table is now regenerated from the result files instead of being maintained by hand. Human enzyme rebuilt as its biological dimer. The deposited coordinates of human glutathione reductase contain a single chain, whereas the flavin site in this enzyme family is formed at the subunit interface. The dimer was reconstructed from the deposition header and re-simulated; binding-mode results for the three dimer replicates are included. Four analyses recomputed under the minimum-image convention. The flavin-to-dyad axis, the ring-stacking geometry, the NADPH occlusion test and the interaction energies had treated the periodic box incorrectly. The files published here come from the corrected versions. Layout. scripts/ holds the analysis code, including scripts/analise_2026-10/ with the routines for the dimer reconstruction, the short equilibration runs, the interaction-energy estimators, the stacking geometry, the flavin-to-dyad axis and the NADPH test. data/ holds the processed result files in JSON. tables/ and figures/ hold the tabulated values and the figure files with their legends. Reuse. The scripts carry absolute paths from the machine they were run on and are published as a record of what was executed rather than as a turnkey pipeline; the trajectories themselves are not included because of their size and are available from the corresponding author on request.

items.summary: Model--harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the persistent yet often overlooked brain--body mismatch problem in this paradigm, where an evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses. We introduce CoEvo-RSI, a RSI framework that advances model--harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. Drawing on a shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent coordinates harness development from historical designs with model checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving execution requirements to reduce brain--body mismatch. Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. It surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant (+14.16 agent accuracy) and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM (+4.90 success rate), underscoring the need for brain--body alignment and the potential of bidirectional historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution.
items.title: CoEvo-RSI: When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?

items.summary: Open radio access network (O-RAN) enables a multi-vendor ecosystem that accelerates xApp development for near-real-time (RT) network management. However, this openness shifts a combinatorial coordination burden to the Non-RT layer, where rApp policies compose xApps from a growing catalog to realize operator intents. Coexisting intents further compound this challenge, as conflicts may arise among xApp actions, rApp policies, and their cross-layer interactions. To maximize intent admission while maintaining key performance indicator (KPI) compliance across incoming and incumbent intents, we propose a large language model-based Multi-Agentic AI framework. A Reasoning Agent screens candidate xApps against KPI contracts and produces a joint intent admission and xApp assignment decision. On post-deployment KPI violations, a Diagnosis Agent identifies the root causes of failure, labels the conflict mechanism, and guides the Reasoning Agent in subsequent attempts. Experimental results show that the framework based on GPT-OSS 120B achieves 28.6% more KPI-compliant cases and admits over 15* as many incoming intents as state-of-the-art baselines. Under the Qwen 72B variant, Diagnosis increases compliant cases by 50.0%, quadruples admitted intents, and reduces deployment attempts by 32.6%. A live deployment conforming to O-RAN specifications further validates the feasibility of the proposed solution for conflict-aware rApp policy orchestration in real networks.
items.title: Multi-Agentic AI for Intent-Driven and Conflict-Aware rApp Policy Orchestration in Open RAN

items.summary: Commit messages provide records of code changes and help developers understand and maintain software. To reduce the manual effort involved in writing them, commit message generation (CMG) approaches automatically generate commit messages that describe code changes in natural language. Existing CMG approaches generally treat CMG as a standalone task and optimize generated messages primarily for similarity to developer-written references. However, this objective may not properly reflect the practical usefulness of generated commit messages. This limitation matters in current AI-assisted software engineering workflows, where commit messages are used as shared information to serve different software engineering activities. To fill this gap, we propose TraceMsg, which uses issue-commit traceability, a representative software engineering activity, to guide commit message generation. TraceMsg is a collaborative multi-agent framework that coordinates message generation, traceability reasoning, and feedback-guided refinement, allowing generated messages to serve traceability while using reasoning feedback to guide issue-conditioned refinement. We evaluate TraceMsg on six open-source projects. The experimental results show that TraceMsg achieves an average Hit@1 of 0.893 and an MRR of 0.911, improving Hit@1 and MRR by 13.16% and 38.75%, respectively, over the best baseline for each metric.
items.title: Beyond Similarity-Based Generation: Guiding Commit Message Generation with Issue-Commit Traceability

items.summary: Archival deposit accompanying A Controlled Audit of a Negative Result: Training Recipe, H.264 Compression Levels and a Frequency-Stream Deepfake Detector , under review at IEEE Access (revision 1). This is version v2.0.2 of the deposit; it goes with release v2.0.2 of the repository. This controlled, self-audited study tests one frequency-based design for compression-robust deepfake detection: CAFRL, which adds block-DCT and FFT-phase streams with compression-conditioned band attention, and an adversarial compression-invariance loss, to an EfficientNet-B0 face backbone. Five separate findings follow. (1) Under the registered rule, CAFRL as specified scored 3.66 AUC points below a backbone-matched EfficientNet-B0 at CRF 40 (paired, one seed). (2) After the audit found eight defects, the control's training recipe recovered 3.96 points for CAFRL's own components (post-audit pre-specified); in a one-seed ablation reverting changes singly, only the backbone learning rate gave an interval excluding zero. (3) At that recipe, these untuned frequency-stream implementations showed no detectable difference from the spatial controls at two feature widths (post-audit pre-specified), yet a standalone frequency head scored 85.27 test-split AUC points at CRF 40 at the selected checkpoints (exploratory). (4) Restoring the adversarial loss at that recipe made no detectable difference in a registered test (0.87 points, Holm-adjusted p = 0.084); the estimator stayed accurate at the selected checkpoints. (5) In registered three-seed tests, real H.264 training levels beat PSNR-matched JPEG versions of the same frames by 7.48 points at CRF 40 (averaged over CRF-40 exposure), and CRF-40-level data added 1.88 points averaged over codec; flat robustness was measured within the trained levels. CAFRL numbers use EMA weights. Evidence: FaceForensics++-family, GAN-era, single-pass H.264 compression. This is version v2.0.2 of the deposit; it goes with release v2.0.2 of the repository. This controlled, self-audited study tests one frequency-based design for compression-robust deepfake detection: CAFRL, which adds block-DCT and FFT-phase streams with compression-conditioned band attention, and an adversarial compression-invariance loss, to an EfficientNet-B0 face backbone. Five separate findings follow. (1) Under the registered rule, CAFRL as specified scored 3.66 AUC points below a backbone-matched EfficientNet-B0 at CRF 40 (paired, one seed). (2) After the audit found eight defects, the control's training recipe recovered 3.96 points for CAFRL's own components (post-audit pre-specified); in a one-seed ablation reverting changes singly, only the backbone learning rate gave an interval excluding zero. (3) At that recipe, these untuned frequency-stream implementations showed no detectable difference from the spatial controls at two feature widths (post-audit pre-specified), yet a standalone frequency head scored 85.27 test-split AUC points at CRF 40 at the selected checkpoints (exploratory). (4) Restoring the adversarial loss at that recipe made no detectable difference in a registered test (0.87 points, Holm-adjusted p = 0.084); the estimator stayed accurate at the selected checkpoints. items.summary: Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce MELD, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. The Coordinator generates a joint portfolio of search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, while Scientists develop hypotheses and execution plans implemented by a shared frozen Executor. Both levels receive alternating GRPO-style parameter updates under a shared smooth best-of-budget objective, allowing team organization and individual research behavior to co-evolve in a recursive self-improvement loop. Our analysis establishes objective alignment for the hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery and the first-order benefit of private adaptation, and derives a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models. On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD is best on 20 of them and achieves the highest aggregate normalized scores on MLGym, using a 4B backbone for coordination and research. Most baselines use proprietary Scientists, and all systems share one frozen Executor.
items.title: MELD: Recursive Self-Improvement via Hierarchical Coordination for Multi-Agent Scientific Discovery

items.summary: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 7% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 87% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly against a single-trajectory GPT-5.6 Sol monitor in at most 25% of executions, compared with 80% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.
items.title: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks

items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to refactor source files, but file-local evaluations do not reveal changes to contracts, dependencies, or caller assumptions affecting repository adoption. To address this gap, we conduct 1,500 generation attempts across 150 production files from 15 open-source Java repositories, five LLM configurations, and two dependency-aware generation conditions: single-prompt refactoring and LangGraph-based multi-agent refactoring. Of these attempts, 1,455 yield complete candidates eligible for analysis. We evaluate these candidates using local changes, repository-facing structural indicators, detected caller impact, the behavioural-equivalence indicator, and available test evidence, and categorize them as Low-risk, Review-needed, High Contract/Dependency Risk, or Inconclusive. The results show that 1,365 candidates (93.8%) are classified as High Contract/Dependency Risk, whereas 106 (7.3%) have at least one detected broken downstream caller and 290 (19.9%) have a false behavioural-equivalence indicator; only eight satisfy the Low-risk criteria. Within the reason-covered subset, the High-risk rate decreases under more conservative dependency-delta thresholds, while 60 of the 65 candidates with conclusive targeted-test outcomes pass, including 50 classified as High risk. Paired analyses of 705 complete pairs identify no statistically significant generation-condition difference in the principal risk indicators, although model configurations differ in specific detected risk channels. These findings suggest that practitioners should treat LLM-generated refactorings as candidates requiring staged repository-level verification, while future research should validate screening and extraction precision and strengthen compilation, behavioural, and coordinated multi-file verification.
items.title: When LLM-Generated Refactorings Ripple: An Empirical Study of Repository Adoption Readiness

items.summary: Multi-agent approaches have been investigated recently as a means of improving the scalability of reinforcement learning for neural combinatorial optimization. Existing methods assume that all problem instance information is known upfront. However, real-world problems are often dynamic: relevant information is progressively revealed as the agents take actions (e.g., arriving at an edge in a routing problem only to discover it is untraversable). In such cases, existing methods fail to coordinate agents to explore and exploit the progressively revealed information. To address the arising coordination challenge, we introduce PACT (Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-graphs). PACT augments the environment graph with auxiliary nodes representing the plans of agents, which are connected to the resource nodes to indicate future dependencies. The proposed message-passing scheme over the augmented graph grounds inter-agent coordination in the environment and enables proactive, rather than reactive, conflict resolution. We show that PACT improves solution quality in dynamic problems relative to baselines and exhibits the best transfer to larger instances on which, remarkably, it outperforms centralized oracles with privileged access to instance uncertainty.
items.title: PACT: Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-Graphs for Dynamic Multi-Agent Combinatorial Optimization

items.summary: As automated research is increasingly adopted for writing papers, automated review has become a critical link between paper generation and quality control. However, existing methods largely rely on single-model feedback or simple review aggregation, failing to explicitly model expert responsibilities or collective deliberation in actual peer reviews, which limits effective cross-examination and reliable decision-making. Therefore, we formulate paper review as a computational modeling problem of peer review mechanisms and propose RoundtableReview, a deliberative multi-agent framework for enhancing automated research. RoundtableReview structures each paper into eight semantic slots and coordinates six academic and industry reviewers with complementary perspectives, retrieval sources, and specialized responsibilities. Through independent assessment, cross-examination, roundtable deliberation, dynamically weighted voting, and chair synthesis, the framework generates evidence-based and traceable feedback. Experiments on two automated research backbones show that the method improves paper quality in both backbones and outperforms baselines in automatic and human evaluations with fewer comments.
items.title: Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review

items.summary: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. Multi-Sequence Verifiers jointly score candidate answers after generation, but the reasoning streams remain independent during inference. ParScale takes a step toward model-internal parallel scaling by learning to aggregate multiple forward passes, but its streams still do not exchange information while processing a sequence. We introduce BatchParScale, an attention mechanism that allows parallel streams to exchange information through a small set of communication positions. We evaluate BatchParScale on a new Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval benchmark and in pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Across these settings, BatchParScale outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks. Masked pretraining runs beat an unmasked single-sequence baseline despite local sequence corruption, and LoRA fine-tuning shows the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer. At the same time, fact retrieval performance for pretrained and finetuned BatchParScale models remains unclear.
items.title: BatchParScale: Sparse Batch-Mixing for Sequence Models

items.summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package supporting the study “Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift.” The study experimentally evaluates a reliability framework for neutron–gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) under controlled operational drift. Rather than proposing a new PSD observable or classifier, the framework distinguishes PSD separability, calibration validity, and decision reliability through controlled perturbation experiments, label-free waveform-health monitoring, identifiability assessment, conditional adaptive recalibration, verification, and fail-safe refusal when the available unlabeled evidence is insufficient to support trusted autonomous correction. The package contains the final analysis and figure-generation scripts, derived numerical tables, and six final manuscript figures. The analyses include independent reconstruction and validation of a frequency-domain classification index (FCI), controlled baseline, gain, additive-noise, timing, and clipping perturbations, label-free degradation diagnosis, identifiability-based recalibration, class-prior robustness testing, and an independent NE213A PSD-domain audit. The primary experimental CLYC–SiPM waveform data are publicly available from Zenodo record 8037239 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.8037239) . The independent NE213A experimental dataset is publicly available from Zenodo record 14305929 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14305929) . Raw experimental data are not redistributed in this package. The NE213A dataset is used as an independent detector- and PSD-domain audit. Waveform-level drift and recovery are deliberately not claimed for NE213A because the acquisition-specific QDC quantities could not be reconstructed from the released waveforms with sufficient held-out fidelity. The repository includes documentation describing data provenance, analysis order, software dependencies, and the scope and limitations of the reproducibility workflow.
items.title: Reproducibility Package for Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift

items.summary: annotations4all is a schema-first Python library for LLM-assisted span annotation, including named entity recognition. Users define their own tag schemas; the library generates chat prompts, parses annotated model responses and maps annotations to character offsets in the original text. The library keeps annotation mechanics separate from research workflows: it bundles no corpus or fixed ontology, performs no evaluation, and does not promise model quality. Provider support uses explicit OpenAI-compatible routes rather than native SDKs. What the library provides Schema-first prompt generation and response parsing. Configurable taggers, German and English prompt templates, metadata-bearing spans and structured parser warnings. Per-label annotation and deterministic merge. Independent label runs can be combined using containment-derived hierarchy, explicit conflict reports and bounded anchoring. One request per run has a corresponding inference cost; merge is not a semantic error repair. Provider policies and capability evidence. A generic OpenAI-compatible client, provider-policy clients, explicit reasoning activation and effort, request limits, packaged hints and offline capability reports. Remote verification requires opt-in; metadata does not prove account access or successful inference. Optional read-only terminal viewer. Browse saved annotations, inspect nested spans and compare two sources using synchronized split or compact diff views. The viewer does not modify annotation files or run inference. Release notes 0.3.1 Request pacing now resolves symlinks in the parent directories of the per-user state file, so a symlinked cache root no longer fails every paced request. The state file keeps its no-follow, regular-file and ownership protection, and cross-process locking is unchanged. Documentation is available in both languages: tutorial and viewer guide each in German and English. Release 0.3.0 introduced provider-policy clients, capability reporting, the optional viewer, data-dependent contrast optimization and deprecation warnings for the legacy native wrappers; the 0.3 notes remain the reference for that feature set. 0.3.1 release notes ; 0.3 feature release notes and screenshots ; initial 0.2 feature baseline . Installation, documentation and verification Python 3.11 or newer. Install with pip install annotations4all==0.3.1 ; add the optional viewer with pip install 'annotations4all[view]==0.3.1' . The tutorial in German and English, the API guides, release notes and screenshot provenance are included with the source archive. items.summary: Code, job scripts and derived results supporting a study of operational water level forecasting for flood monitoring in Lamphun, northern Thailand. Five compact single-hidden-layer neural networks forecast hourly stage 6 to 18 hours ahead at three gauges (P.5, P.87, P.85), each paired with an upstream gauge. The record contains the open-source NumPy (Levenberg–Marquardt) ANN on which all retrospective results are based, evaluated on 65 leave-one-flood-year-out blocks (configurations from an earlier MATLAB experiment published separately); benchmarks against persistence, a linear model given the same inputs, XGBoost, and long short-term memory (LSTM) and GRU networks with a sensitivity analysis; leakage checks (predictor selection by LASSO repeated inside every block, whole-year early stopping, an antecedent-rainfall candidate pool); Diebold–Mariano tests, a datum-independent Kling–Gupta efficiency, threshold exceedance scores, skill by flow state, upstream travel time and a scan for frozen gauge records; and the reference code and a 76-day evaluation (2 August–17 October 2026) of the deployed hourly forecasting and alerting service. Summary results for every table and figure are included, with a synthetic example dataset that demonstrates the input format and evaluation code. items.summary: annotations-orchestration is a Python library for configuring and running LLM annotation and evaluation experiments. It combines a resumable, manifest-driven scheduler with an optional terminal editor and a declarative annotation runner. Span metrics are computed by annotations-evaluate ; annotation clients, taggers, provider capabilities and hints come from annotations4all . Scope and architecture Base scheduler: experiment YAMLs and optional controller manifests define runs, defaults, execution settings and ordering. The default legacy runner uses a subprocess CLI contract and does not require an annotation library. Optional editor: the tui extra provides annotations-tui , a Textual editor for single-run and multi-run experiments and controllers. Editing, inspection and effective-run previews do not execute experiments. Optional standard runner: the annotate extra uses annotations4all>=0.3.1,<1 to annotate from a declarative annotation block without a custom consumer frontend. Metrics: this package adapts run records and writes reports; it does not implement metric counting. Run reports use the SemEval-compatible flat scenarios of annotations-evaluate ; that library also provides a nested standard report. Release notes 0.3.0 This release adds the editor, standard runner and provider-aware configuration layer to the 0.2 scheduler. Existing state files, PID locks, graceful shutdown, resume planning, manifest-key validation and the metric definitions remain supported. Manifest editor: structured forms, full YAML editing and effective-run previews share a common side-effect-free resolver with the CLI. New, duplicate, remove, reorder and Save As workflows preserve comments and quotes where supported. Saves show a diff and use atomic replacement with conflict detection; ambiguous YAML falls back to raw editing. Read-only mode and unsaved-change dialogs protect documents. Inheritance and responsive forms: Experiment → Defaults → Runs shows effective values and their origin without materializing inherited overrides. New runs stay empty. Legacy-header migration requires explicit diff confirmation. Run cards group model/prompting, annotation/input and connection settings. Provider/model configuration: a packaged catalog and startup-directory overlay provide presets and manual IDs. Explicit Refresh reads metadata only for the selected provider/key context. Capability evidence is field-specific and session-only; custom endpoints require trust confirmation before receiving a key. Credentials and display: the editor manages only the startup directory's .env , masks values and uses explicit atomic writes. Secrets do not enter manifests, settings or diffs. F9 controls NerdFont icons and persistent themes; --theme overrides the session and Ctrl+P opens the command palette. Reasoning and hints: reasoning and effort are separate inherited fields. Contradictory settings are rejected; live-reported effort choices constrain selection while incompatible stored values remain diagnostic. Contextual hints cite sources and change no settings. Declarative annotation: runner: standard supports configurable and per-label tagging with schema-validated label/description pairs, context, German or English prompts and message splitting. A no-inference preflight validates inputs and a fresh output destination. Input and gold semantics: the runner and directory inspector share non-mutating normalization for top-level Prodigy spans and ground_truth.prodigy/tags . Missing gold produces an annotation-only completion; explicitly empty gold remains evaluable. Conflicting gold representations are rejected before inference. Scheduling and pacing: ordinary remote runs share a configurable pool; self-hosted runs are sequential per host. The exact HU endpoint has a dedicated serial lane capped at 10 requests per minute, independent of scheduling mode. items.summary: Data, pre-registrations and code for “Size and Chemical Contributions to the Cauchy Deviation of Cubic Oxide Perovskites” This record contains the data, pre-registration files, calculation notebooks and analysis scripts for a study of the Cauchy deviation C12 − C44 of ideal cubic (Pm-3m) oxide perovskites ABO3. In this structure every atom sits at a centre of inversion, so C12 − C44 is a relaxation-free, net measure of non-central cohesion. The study was carried out in five sequentially pre-registered stages. For each stage, the hypotheses and decision rules were written and checksummed (SHA-256) before the calculations of that stage: Screening of 64 cubic compositions with the universal machine-learned potential MACE-MP-0. DFT-PBE tests of chemistry-specific contributions (8 compounds: Pb2+ lone pair, In3+ versus Sc3+, A-site size in A+B5+O3). DFT-PBE test of the size dependence in 18 A2+B4+O3 perovskites (A = Ca, Sr, Ba; B = Ti, Zr, Hf, Sn, Ge, Si). PBEsol functional control (7 compounds). Numerical convergence tests and the R25 octahedral-rotation stiffness of the 18 compounds. DFT calculations: Quantum ESPRESSO 7.6, SSSP 1.3.0 efficiency pseudopotentials, stress–strain elastic constants at the equilibrium lattice parameter. All calculations were run on Google Colab. Main results: at fixed B, C12 − C44 decreases with the A-cation radius in all six families, while the B-cation radius sets the level of each family. A two-radius model gives a leave-one-family-out R² of 0.88, against 0.81 for the Goldschmidt tolerance factor. The Pb2+ lone pair and In3+ add positive contributions above this size baseline. C12 − C44 is insensitive to the functional and converged to better than 1 GPa. Within families, the R25 stiffness follows the A-site trend and cannot be separated from it. MACE-MP-0 overestimates C12 − C44 by about 18 GPa and misses the within-family trend in four of six families. Contents: stage1_mace/ to stage5_convergence_rotation/: pre-registration files with their checksums, results (CSV/JSON), notebooks and scripts for each stage; review_statistics/: post hoc analyses (family-cluster bootstrap, leave-one-family-out validation, model comparison); dft_raw_outputs/: Quantum ESPRESSO output files; README.md (folder map, how to verify the checksums), SHA256SUMS.txt.

items.summary: As automated research is increasingly adopted for writing papers, automated review has become a critical link between paper generation and quality control. However, existing methods largely rely on single-model feedback or simple review aggregation, failing to explicitly model expert responsibilities or collective deliberation in actual peer reviews, which limits effective cross-examination and reliable decision-making. Therefore, we formulate paper review as a computational modeling problem of peer review mechanisms and propose RoundtableReview, a deliberative multi-agent framework for enhancing automated research. RoundtableReview structures each paper into eight semantic slots and coordinates six academic and industry reviewers with complementary perspectives, retrieval sources, and specialized responsibilities. Through independent assessment, cross-examination, roundtable deliberation, dynamically weighted voting, and chair synthesis, the framework generates evidence-based and traceable feedback. Experiments on two automated research backbones show that the method improves paper quality in both backbones and outperforms baselines in automatic and human evaluations with fewer comments.
items.title: Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review

items.summary: Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning. With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability. We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification. We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions. On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances. In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%. Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced. Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.
items.title: Policy Search in Code Space for Multi-Agent Pathfinding

items.summary: Data, pre-registrations and code for “Size and Chemical Contributions to the Cauchy Deviation of Cubic Oxide Perovskites” This record contains the data, pre-registration files, calculation notebooks and analysis scripts for a study of the Cauchy deviation C12 − C44 of ideal cubic (Pm-3m) oxide perovskites ABO3. In this structure every atom sits at a centre of inversion, so C12 − C44 is a relaxation-free, net measure of non-central cohesion. The study was carried out in five sequentially pre-registered stages. For each stage, the hypotheses and decision rules were written and checksummed (SHA-256) before the calculations of that stage: Screening of 64 cubic compositions with the universal machine-learned potential MACE-MP-0. DFT-PBE tests of chemistry-specific contributions (8 compounds: Pb2+ lone pair, In3+ versus Sc3+, A-site size in A+B5+O3). DFT-PBE test of the size dependence in 18 A2+B4+O3 perovskites (A = Ca, Sr, Ba; B = Ti, Zr, Hf, Sn, Ge, Si). PBEsol functional control (7 compounds). Numerical convergence tests and the R25 octahedral-rotation stiffness of the 18 compounds. DFT calculations: Quantum ESPRESSO 7.6, SSSP 1.3.0 efficiency pseudopotentials, stress–strain elastic constants at the equilibrium lattice parameter. All calculations were run on Google Colab. Main results: at fixed B, C12 − C44 decreases with the A-cation radius in all six families, while the B-cation radius sets the level of each family. A two-radius model gives a leave-one-family-out R² of 0.88, against 0.81 for the Goldschmidt tolerance factor. The Pb2+ lone pair and In3+ add positive contributions above this size baseline. C12 − C44 is insensitive to the functional and converged to better than 1 GPa. Within families, the R25 stiffness follows the A-site trend and cannot be separated from it. MACE-MP-0 overestimates C12 − C44 by about 18 GPa and misses the within-family trend in four of six families. Contents: stage1_mace/ to stage5_convergence_rotation/: pre-registration files with their checksums, results (CSV/JSON), notebooks and scripts for each stage; review_statistics/: post hoc analyses (family-cluster bootstrap, leave-one-family-out validation, model comparison); dft_raw_outputs/: Quantum ESPRESSO output files; README.md (folder map, how to verify the checksums), SHA256SUMS.txt.

items.summary: Six independent 100 ns molecular dynamics trajectories of human acetylcholinesterase (PDB 4EY7) in complex with two ligands: donepezil, whose dual-site binding mode is established crystallographically in that structure, and N-(1-benzylpiperidin-4-yl)-2-phenyl-1H-benzimidazole-5-carboxamide (DAH-004). Three trajectories per ligand were generated from the same equilibrated structure under identical parameters, differing only in the initial velocity distribution. The deposit contains the production trajectories (water and ions removed, 200 ps sampling), the GROMACS run input files, twelve minimum-distance time series to Trp86 and Trp286 computed with gmx pairdist, the per-window contact occupancy table, and the scripts that generate the figures of the associated manuscript. Software: GROMACS 2026.0, AMBER99SB-ILDN, GAFF2 with AM1-BCC charges, TIP3P water. This version adds the excursion-kinetics analysis: Figure 4 and the script that generates it from the twelve minimum-distance time series.
